entries.guidedDefinition: A property of a phenomenon, body, or substance that has a magnitude expressible as a number and a reference; length is a quantity, while 2 metres is a quantity value.
entries.technicalDefinition: The Tour uses physical quantity for the VIM concept quantity: a scalar property with a magnitude expressible as a number and a reference. A quantity is not its quantity value, numerical value, kind, dimension, or unit.

caveats: The guided definition is scoped to scalar quantities used in this lesson.

entries.guidedDefinition: A number together with a reference that expresses the magnitude of a quantity, such as 2 m for a particular length.
entries.technicalDefinition: The number-and-reference expression of a quantity's magnitude. The reference is usually a measurement unit but can also be a measurement procedure, reference material, or combination.

entries.guidedDefinition: The number in a quantity value after choosing its reference; the same length has numerical value 2 in metres and 200 in centimetres.
entries.technicalDefinition: The number in the expression of a quantity value, other than any number serving as the reference. It changes under a unit conversion even though the quantity does not.

entries.guidedDefinition: The common aspect of quantities that makes them mutually comparable, such as length or thermodynamic temperature.
entries.technicalDefinition: The VIM kind of quantity concept groups mutually comparable quantities. Equal dimensions are necessary but not sufficient for the same kind: energy and torque share a dimension but are different kinds of quantity.

caveats: Dimension equality alone does not establish quantity-kind identity.

entries.guidedDefinition: A conventionally defined quantity used as a reference for quantities of the same kind.
entries.technicalDefinition: A real scalar quantity defined and adopted by convention with which another quantity of the same kind is compared to express their ratio as a number.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update

entries.guidedDefinition: A description of how a quantity depends on chosen base quantities, written with powers such as length divided by time.
entries.technicalDefinition: An expression of a quantity kind's dependence on the base quantities of a system as a product of powers. Equal dimensions do not by themselves establish equal quantity kinds; energy and torque are a standard counterexample.

caveats: The basis is conventional.

entries.guidedDefinition: A quantity whose physical dimensions cancel, often a ratio of like quantities.
entries.technicalDefinition: A quantity with the zero dimension vector; its value can still depend on conventions such as angle units or normalization.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update
caveats: Dimensionless does not mean convention-free.

entries.guidedDefinition: Corresponding terms in an equation have matching dimensions, which is necessary but does not prove they have the same quantity kind or that the equation is true.
entries.technicalDefinition: Every additive term has the same dimension vector and both sides transform covariantly under a multiplicative coherent unit change. This necessary check is not a sufficient quantity-kind or empirical-validity test.

attribution.sourceRevision: JCGM 200:2012; NIST SP 811e2008
attribution.sourceLocator: VIM3 entries 1.2, 1.7, and 1.21; NIST SP 811 chapters 7-8
caveats: Consistency is necessary, not sufficient for empirical validity.

entries.guidedDefinition: The collection of units used to write the numerical values of quantities.
entries.technicalDefinition: A basis choice in quantity space; changing basis transforms numerical coordinates while preserving the underlying quantity. An exact nominal astronomical conversion constant changes coordinates but does not make a body's measured property exact.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update; IAU 2015 Resolution B3
attribution.sourceLocator: BIPM section 2.3; IAU Resolution B3 nominal conversion constants
caveats: The phrase is Tour shorthand for a declared unit basis.
Nominal astronomical conversion constants are not measured properties.

entries.guidedDefinition: One of the conventionally chosen base-quantity dimensions used to express other dimensions.
entries.technicalDefinition: A conventional basis element of a system of quantity dimensions. The Tour uses the seven conventional base-quantity dimensions of the International System of Quantities (ISQ) and permits rational exponents generally; this activity uses only integer exponents.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update; JCGM 200:2012
caveats: Technical-only term; Guided blocks must not depend on it.

entries.guidedDefinition: A coordinate choice that uses important physical constants as reference scales.
entries.technicalDefinition: A unit convention setting selected dimensional constants, often c, hbar, or k_B, to numerical unity without erasing their dimensional role.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update
caveats: Technical-only term; Guided blocks must not depend on it.

entries.guidedDefinition: An ideal object that absorbs all incident radiation and emits a thermal spectrum determined only by its thermodynamic temperature.
entries.technicalDefinition: An idealized absorber with absorptivity one at every wavelength and direction; at thermal equilibrium its emitted spectral distribution is the Planck distribution. The Tour's simulation fixes emissivity to one and does not model a material surface.

attribution.sourceRevision: OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, 2016 web edition accessed 2026-07-27
caveats: Real sources generally depart from the ideal through emissivity, geometry, environment, and instrument response.

entries.guidedDefinition: A comparison of how strongly a real surface emits thermal radiation with how strongly an ideal black body would emit at the same temperature.
entries.technicalDefinition: A dimensionless ratio of a surface's emitted radiometric quantity to the corresponding black-body quantity at the same thermodynamic temperature, with spectral, directional, or hemispherical scope stated as applicable.

attribution.sourceRevision: OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, 2016 web edition accessed 2026-07-27
attribution.sourceLocator: Section 6.1, ideal and real thermal emitters
caveats: Emissivity can depend on wavelength, direction, polarization, temperature, and surface condition.

entries.guidedDefinition: A physical quantity that orders thermal states and sets thermal energy scales; its SI unit is the kelvin.
entries.technicalDefinition: The base quantity T of the International System of Quantities for thermodynamic temperature. Its SI unit, the kelvin, is defined by fixing the numerical value of the Boltzmann constant k_B.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update; IUPAC Green Book, 3rd edition, corrected 2nd printing
caveats: A temperature-equivalent energy scale does not by itself identify a thermodynamic state.

entries.guidedDefinition: Radiant power described per projected emitting area, per viewing direction, and per wavelength or frequency interval.
entries.technicalDefinition: Radiance density with respect to a declared spectral coordinate. The simulation uses wavelength spectral radiance B_lambda in W m^-3 sr^-1; changing to B_nu requires the spectral-coordinate Jacobian and changes the peak coordinate.

attribution.sourceRevision: OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, 2016 web edition accessed 2026-07-27; IUPAC Green Book, 3rd edition, corrected 2nd printing
attribution.sourceLocator: OpenStax section 6.1; IUPAC radiometric quantities and units
caveats: Wavelength-domain and frequency-domain spectral radiance are different densities.

entries.guidedDefinition: The total radiant power leaving a surface per unit emitting area.
entries.technicalDefinition: Radiant flux emitted into the outward hemisphere divided by source area, measured in W m^-2. For an ideal black body integrated over all wavelengths, M = sigma T^4.

attribution.sourceRevision: OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, 2016 web edition accessed 2026-07-27; IUPAC Green Book, 3rd edition, corrected 2nd printing
attribution.sourceLocator: OpenStax section 6.1, Stefan law; IUPAC radiometric quantities
caveats: Exitance is hemispherically integrated and is not the same quantity as directional radiance.

entries.guidedDefinition: For an ideal black-body wavelength spectrum, the peak wavelength moves inversely with thermodynamic temperature.
entries.technicalDefinition: The wavelength-domain Planck distribution satisfies lambda_max T = b, where b is the Wien wavelength displacement constant. This maximum is not the reciprocal coordinate of the frequency-domain maximum.

attribution.sourceRevision: OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, 2016 web edition accessed 2026-07-27; CODATA 2022 adjustment
attribution.sourceLocator: OpenStax section 6.1; CODATA Wien wavelength displacement constant
caveats: The stated law and constant apply to the wavelength-form spectrum.

entries.guidedDefinition: An ideal black body's total emitted radiant power per area grows as the fourth power of thermodynamic temperature.
entries.technicalDefinition: The all-wavelength radiant exitance of an ideal black body is M = sigma T^4. A real surface requires an appropriately defined emissivity and may not follow a single-temperature ideal spectrum.

attribution.sourceRevision: OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, 2016 web edition accessed 2026-07-27; CODATA 2022 adjustment
caveats: The ideal law is not a material-emissivity or measured-source model.

entries.guidedDefinition: A physical quantity that counts specified elementary entities by using the mole as its unit.
entries.technicalDefinition: The ISQ base quantity n proportional to the number N of specified elementary entities, with N = n N_A. It is distinct from the dimensionless entity count N and requires the entity to be specified.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update; IUPAC Green Book, 3rd edition, corrected 2nd printing
caveats: Amount of substance is not interchangeable with a bare entity count.

entries.guidedDefinition: The SI unit of amount of substance; one mole contains exactly 6.022 140 76 x 10^23 specified elementary entities.
entries.technicalDefinition: The SI base unit mol. One mole contains exactly N_A = 6.02214076 x 10^23 specified elementary entities because the Avogadro constant has the fixed numerical value 6.02214076 x 10^23 mol^-1.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update
caveats: The current definition fixes an entity count, not the mass of one mole of carbon-12.

entries.guidedDefinition: The specified particle, atom, molecule, ion, electron, or defined group being counted by an amount of substance.
entries.technicalDefinition: An entity that must be specified when amount of substance is stated; it may be an atom, molecule, ion, electron, another particle, or a specified group of such particles.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update; IUPAC Green Book, 3rd edition, corrected 2nd printing
caveats: Different specified entities are not interchangeable counts.

entries.guidedDefinition: The exact number of specified entities per mole, N_A = 6.022 140 76 x 10^23 mol^-1.
entries.technicalDefinition: The SI defining constant N_A with fixed exact numerical value 6.02214076 x 10^23 when expressed in mol^-1; it connects entity count and amount through N = n N_A.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update
caveats: An exact N_A does not make a user-supplied amount or sample composition exact.

entries.guidedDefinition: The mass of a substance divided by its amount of substance, usually expressed in kilograms per mole or grams per mole.
entries.technicalDefinition: The molar quantity M = m/n with SI unit kg mol^-1. It depends on the specified substance and composition and, in the current SI, is not fixed exactly by the definition of the mole.

attribution.sourceRevision: IUPAC Green Book, 3rd edition, corrected 2nd printing; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update
attribution.sourceLocator: IUPAC section 2.10; BIPM section 2.3.3 and mole notes
caveats: Isotopic composition, mixtures, association, and impurities can affect the applicable molar mass.

entries.guidedDefinition: A model gas whose pressure, volume, amount, and thermodynamic temperature obey p V = n R T.
entries.technicalDefinition: A limiting equation-of-state model with pV = nRT, neglecting intermolecular interactions and finite molecular volume. Real-gas use requires checking the state range and non-ideal corrections.

attribution.sourceRevision: IUPAC Green Book, 3rd edition, corrected 2nd printing
attribution.sourceLocator: Section 2.11, gas equations and thermodynamic quantities
caveats: The ideal-gas equation does not establish that a real sample is ideal at a selected state.

entries.guidedDefinition: A pressure convention equal exactly to 101 325 pascals, written 1 atm.
entries.technicalDefinition: The non-SI pressure unit standard atmosphere, symbol atm, defined exactly as 101325 Pa. It is not a measured ambient pressure and does not by itself define a complete thermodynamic standard state.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update; IUPAC Green Book, 3rd edition, corrected 2nd printing
attribution.sourceLocator: BIPM non-SI pressure-unit table; IUPAC section 4.3
caveats: One atmosphere is distinct from 100000 Pa and from an unstated ambient pressure.

entries.guidedDefinition: An explicit choice of conditions, such as temperature and pressure, used when quoting a state-dependent quantity.
entries.technicalDefinition: Tour shorthand for a declared set of thermodynamic reference conditions. A gas volume must carry its selected temperature, pressure, composition, and model rather than relying on an ambiguous label such as standard conditions.

attribution.sourceRevision: IUPAC Green Book, 3rd edition, corrected 2nd printing
attribution.sourceLocator: Sections 2.11 and 4.3, thermodynamic and standard-state conventions
caveats: The phrase is Tour shorthand; the actual temperature, pressure, composition, and model must be stated.

entries.guidedDefinition: The electric-charge magnitude carried by one mole of singly charged entities, F = N_A e.
entries.technicalDefinition: The molar elementary charge F = N_A e with SI unit C mol^-1. Because N_A and e have fixed exact SI values, F is exact in the current SI; Q = z n F additionally requires a signed charge number z.

attribution.sourceRevision: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, 2026 update; CODATA 2022 adjustment
attribution.sourceLocator: Fixed N_A and e; CODATA Faraday constant entry
caveats: The conversion does not establish reaction completion, charge-transfer efficiency, or measured current.
